card: This PR integrates Bitcoin Core's hardware-accelerated SHA256 compression function into libsecp256k1 context instances, replacing libsecp256k1's software-only hashing fallback. It also separates ECC context initialization into dedicated signing and verification contexts managed via a unified RAII lifecycle. Benchmarks show a 7% to 13% reduction in signing latency on architectures with SHA hardware extensions, while verification performance remains essentially unchanged. No prerequisite or dependent pull requests are indicated.
changed_since_previous: The underlying approach and commit progression remain consistent with the prior description; changes reflect rebasing and test/benchmark adjustments.
evidence: PR description benchmarks on ARM64 with SHA-NI show ECDSA signing time drops from 79.2 µs to 69.3 µs (-13%) and Schnorr signing drops from 39.9 µs to 37.1 µs (-7%).
Commit 3104f72514 notes: 'With ours, ECDSA signing gets ~15% faster on CPUs with SHA extensions, Schnorr signing ~3%.' Verification benchmarks show negligible improvement (0% to -1%).
problem: libsecp256k1 uses its internal pure-software SHA256 compression implementation by default, bypassing available CPU hardware acceleration (such as x86 SHA-NI and ARMv8 cryptography extensions) during elliptic curve signing and verification. Additionally, `secp256k1_context_static` cannot be configured with custom compression hooks, and ECC initialization was tightly coupled to `key.h` primitives.

risk.why: A flaw in the SHA256 compression callback or context initialization could cause silent signature creation errors or misvalidate cryptographic checks across the node.

scope_notes: A significant portion of the 44 changed files is mechanical: updating fuzz targets, benchmarks, and binaries to initialize ECC state via `MakeContextECC()`, plus a scripted-diff substituting `secp256k1_context_static` with `GetSecp256k1VerifyContext()` in `src/pubkey.cpp`.
summary: Plugs Bitcoin Core's hardware-accelerated SHA256 compression function into libsecp256k1 contexts. It restructures `ECC_Context` into a lifecycle manager that provides both signing and verification contexts, moves ECC initialization into `common/ecc_init`, and updates call sites to use the new verification context instead of `secp256k1_context_static`.
